Question: What was a feudal army?
Answer: A feudal army was an army in which the organization of the military was according to the feudal hierarchy of the society. That means that the ranking liege lord, would summon his vassals, who in turn would summon their vassals all the way down to the peasant bondsmen. The King of Denmark firetaxing (extorting) Visby after the Danish defeated the Swedish in 1361 It is often considered that a feudal army was an elite cavalry force surrounded by low quality infantry levies. However, that is not nessesarily the nature of feudalism, though it is partially true for some west European kingdoms. A king might call upon his duke, counts and barons, who personally will fight as elite mounted warriors. However the main stay of the army varies entirely on which companies the vassal choose to keep. The English famously maintained pretty skilled archers who were by no means low quality. The French were able to field almost entire armies of professional warriors and mercenaries. Other kingdoms called upon free cities to provide trained companies of engineers and crossbowmen such as Bercelona. The core of a feudal army then is simply that it is made up of vassal obligations, but what that army actually consists of in practice depended on regional specialties and effort put into maintaining their men at arms.

The Soviets had 228 divisions against the western allied 80. Though Soviet divisions were about 17% smaller than US divisions. It had just defeated Nazism, and unlike today, this was pretty much undisputed at the time. Communists were slated to win elections in places like France and Italy, and Labour did win in Great Britain. Western countries were rightfully scared of the massive backing communism and the USSR enjoyed from their own populations. If an attack on the USSR had been made, it would be betraying a current ally in the worst of ways, and most people would have been quite upset over this, not just the communists. So the surprise attack would have been conducted without nukes. Additionally, 2 nukes would have very little tactical impact on the battlefield, it would however have massive repercussions politically. Question: Why is the Axis defeat at Stalingrad (1942/43) viewed as the turning point of WWII? Operation Bagration (1944) caused more German casualties, Army Group Center was destroyed, and the Soviets pushed the Germans out of Russia completely.
Answer: It is viewed as the turning point because it was in the sense that after Stalingrad Germany no longer had the initiative on the eastern front, and everything they did from there on was merely a reacting to the Soviets who had the control. You could also view it thusly: Moscow proved Germany could be stopped, Stalingrad proved Germany could be defeated, Kursk proved Germany could no longer attack, definitively putting them on the defensive for the rest of the war. Bagration was the largest and most complete victory for the Soviets without a doubt, but at that point the Soviets were in a much better position. The Soviets won the battle of Stalingrad, despite the desperate nature of the battle. Despite the defeats in Ukraine in the same year. Despite the low manpower and resources available to the Soviets in November 1942. This is the time when the Soviets overcame these difficulties. They managed to apply a heavy economy or force, concentrate and build up a critical mass, confuse and surprise the enemy, use effective intelligence and destroy a large part of his forces. But it was a massively costly victory, and not a total one either, as the Soviets failed to destroy the German Caucasus army. It did however knock out most of the axis support that Germany had, from Italy, Hungary and Romania, which was a crucial step in reducing their presence on the eastern front. While Bagration was indeed more impressive, it was a more comfortable situation, where Soviet superiority over German forces was essentially undisputed. Not that it was not hard fought, but Stalingrad was the most intense single operation in history in terms of manpower and equipment lost, and set up the remainder of the eastern front.

Question: What is wrong with the American Abrams tank, and why are the Ukrainians losing them?
Answer: There are some things wrong with the Abrams tank, despite the endless optimism. Reading most other answers, one would think that the Abrams was perfectly suited for modern operations in Ukraine against drones, despite being designed for fighting in Germany in 1980s against other tanks. There are in fact flaws to the design, the tank has strengths and weaknesses. The most and most obvious thing that’s wrong with the Abrams, is that it is too heavy. It is a really heavy tank, and due to excessive eating it has only gained weight since 1980. The tank was designed originally at 55t, due to attempts at adding more armor to the tank and other upgrades, the M1A2 Sepv3 is estimated to sit at around 73t. The engine compartment has not gotten bigger. Even the older models without DU armor are heavy vehicles. And it has many disadvantages, firstly it does not fit on to the common 50t railroad flat bed cars, which is a logistical problem. Secondly, it does not do well with heavily muddied areas because its ground pressure is massive. Thirdly, it is unable to cross some bridges due to weight limits. Fourthly, the weight means that components of the Abrams require more maintenance and is under more stress than on lighter tanks. Finally, the heavy tank is difficult to tow for other tanks, meaning only a few specialized recovery vehicles can do it. All this weight unfortunately, has not gone where it is needed most, which is the top. Despite around 15t of additional protective upgrades, none of the M1 Abrams ever received anything to make them more difficult to destroy from the top. This means the original M1 Abrams and the newest M1 Abrams are equally vulnerable to drones, DPICM and other top attack weapons. The already excessive weight might also be one of the reasons why no one has added additional armor to the top in the form of cages. The M1 is not a bad tank, but it has design flaws, it was not build to do what it is doing now, it could be better, in fact a drastically different design would be a better option than just adding more weight on this tank. There are several other comparative disadvantageous of the Abrams to some of its competitors, but I think this is enough to point out why it might not feel so hot right now. It’s probably quite a challenge to fight from the front in a tank duel, but what does it matter if it is getting stuck in mud due to its weight, getting destroyed by cheap drones or getting tracked by artillery before it ever gets in range of other tanks?

So you can see despite being the same amount of bomb, the more but smaller bombs is actually better at destroying something by area. That’s not a incident pressure, that is fragmented steel traveling through a dusin layers of wall, and creating additional impact shrapnel through each wall inside those rooms. This building is still standing, but the inside is completely shredded, though this is not so obvious from the air. Finally, we have the ODAB variant. The thermobaric variants give up the ability to create a lot of high penetration shrapnel, in favor of creating a bigger pressure zone, and also adding an incendiary and non-linear direction of effect. That means, that the ODAB variants, tend to generate almost twice as big zones of destruction as their conventional RDX/HMX based counter parts, some thermobaric compounds are alleged to be 4 times more powerful than TNT (C-4 is 1.6 times more powerful). These bombs spread an explosive aerosol over an area then detonates it, this has the massive advantage that the aerosol can get inside buildings and other areas like bunkers or buildings, before detonating. This exponentially increases their ability to demolish, as well as almost guaranteeing termination of all life in the area, no matter what kind of cover is provided. No ODAB-3000 exists as far as I am aware. Due to their function thermobaric explosives scale a lot better than conventional ones do, and can cover massive areas with their aerosols if there is enough of it. The Russian FOAB would probably be an ODAB-7000, at this scale the FOAB allegedly provides the power of 44t of TNT, which is twice as much as the Davy Crocket mini nuclear weapon. Question: What year were the first MBTs (Main Battle Tanks) deployed? How do they differ from modern MBTs?
Answer: Main Battle Tank (MBT) is not actually a real classification of tank. The MBT of a country is quite simply the main tank they use hence the name. This is almost always a medium tank and for most of the cold war literature it was referred to as such in the west. When the Soviets built the T-72 and T-64 tanks they were also designed under the name medium tank, because it was designated by mass. The Soviet themselves switched to classifying tanks as Main Tank and Special Tank, while in general, the idea of Main Battle Tank was formalized by the 1990 convention: “Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe”, aimed at reducing the presence of weapons. Certain island dwellers are entirely convinced the Centurion was the first MBT. This convention defined it as an Armored Fighting Vehicle (AFV), which has By this definition a T-34 or M3 Lee could be considered a main battle tank. The Chieftain which people often point to as being the first MBT was designed under the name of Medium Gun Tank No. 2. The designation o MBT was simply added retroactively, as well as for the centurion. In reality the MBT designation doesn’t tell you anything about a tank’s capabilities.

Question: In wwii, during the battle of stalingrad, could the soviets have destroyed both the German 6th army and the rest of army group south? What prevented that, and did the red army have that capability at that point in the war?
Answer: They did have this capability and the original plan Called “Operation Saturn” had exactly the goal of reaching Rostov on Don, which would have cut off all the German forces in the south. However, this plan hinged on the quickly surrender or defeat of the German forces in the Stalingrad pocket, which was estimated at 80,000 troops. It turned out it was over 250,000 troops, and the fighting would continue not just in December but through January as well. This meant that operation Saturn was cancelled as significant Soviet forces were tied up in cleaning and containing the encirclement, additionally Mannstein launched a rescue attempt to relieve the pocket. This further exhausted the Soviet striking forces in the area. The Soviets still had pretty significant forces available, but the plan was deemed too risky with events not unfolding exactly as expected. Having suffered serious defeats in the previous years, the Soviets were wary not to over extend. Finally, the Soviets did not have enough trucks to launch deep offensive of the length which was required for to reach Rostov on Don without doing start stops, this meant they would need to follow the railroads which made their path predictable and therefore easier to ambush. This was to be a decisive victory, and launching a risky grand offensive under these conditions was not something the Soviet general had a stomach for, despite the poor state of German forces meant it was technically possible. Instead the Soviets opted for a smaller offensive, called Little Saturn, seen on the map above. This offensive aimed at eliminating the weaker Axis allies near Stalingrad, namely the 3rd Romanian army and the 8th Italian army. It was partially successful in this, knocking out about 100,000 troops. It was followed up by the Voronezh–Kharkov offensive, which was hugely successful knocking out 250,000 troops more for just 37,000 losses. This resulted in the elimination of the Hungarian and Italian armies on the eastern front more or less. These offensives were not as risky, but ultimately destroyed nearly as many Axis troops as the Stalingrad offensive itself, and did so with minimal casualties. It’s a very over looked scenario, that panned out pretty well and it was almost certainly the right choice to use the resources like so, rather than trying to cut off the southern German army group.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: If the Nazis defeated the Soviets prior to Dday, what would have happened in the Pacific? Would the allies fight on two fronts? Sue for peace? Would the Nazis come to the aid of Japan? What other scenarios may have occurred?
Answer: This was an impossible outcome. The best possible outcome that Germany could have hoped for in their wildest dreams, was that the USSR would simply give up and accept a terrible peace deal in which Russia west of the Urals became part of Nazi Germany. Even in such a far fetched case, Germany would still not even be able to get to Japan if they wanted to. Robert Harris imagined in his book Fatherland, a situation in which Germany would still be having a perpetual war against the Soviets even in 1964. More likely though, Germany now occupied a gigantic territory, and even with the vastly reduced population they intended, they were facing down something close to 100 million people with nothing to lose. Even if Soviet industry completely ceased to exist, which is quite unlikely as much of it was already beyond the Urals, the USSR would continue fighting with what ever they had, even if they had to rely 100% on lend-lease they could still fight. This leaves the question, how many people did the Germans need to occupy and protect their new eastern border? The answer is certainly quite a lot. Additionally, Japan as a naval power was finished after Midway, their losses in 1942 were irrecoverable for Japan, and their defeat was merely a matter of time. Even if the western allies were forced to defeat Japan first, and then focus on supplying the Soviet remnant, and plan a new invasion of Europe in 1946 or something like that. They could have, and would have done so. Also there is the matter that the allies would almost certainly have nuked Germany in 1945. No matter how I see it, the Axis powers had sealed their ultimate fate in 1941, both the USSR and USA had the capacity to defeat Nazi Germany alone. Without each other, the war would have been longer, harder, deadlier a worse outcome without a doubt. But Nazi defeat still remained a certainty, the question was mostly about the human cost of the show.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Do you have any favorite “flaws” with Warhammer 40,000?
Answer: I quite like warhammer, ever since I played the original Dawn of War game as a kid, I went as far as reading several of the books which are often actually very accomplished sci-fi novels in their own right, but the one thing that probably is the most consistently hilarious is the total refusal to accept the scale of things that is mentioned in the books. Now, the authors are probably severely limited by the constraints of the table top models, basically forcing players to have relatively few troops. Never the less, it is almost amusing how important individuals and tiny groups of people are. For example in the Eisenhorn novel, the Inquisition launches a planetary invasion of a Xenos world, they are aided by the deathwatch who sends a whopping 60 space marines, spread out as well. Space marine chapters are in the thousands, legions were about 100,000 on average. Dear Gamesworkshop, the current military force of Earth is about 27–28 million soldiers. It’s not even a matter of how great space marines are, 100,000 space marines would take thousands of years to cover a small planet with their presence. Now some of the novels makes it clear that this is all part of an elaborate combined arms assault, some of them don’t. Consider also that the Imperial palace on Terra is supposed to be a little over 1.1 million square kilometer, it is protected by 10,000 adeptus custodes, that’s about 1 guard for 112 square kilometer. Good luck. In one of the newest books, Terra losses control over the beacon built into mount Everest, as the entire place is more or less taken over by rebels and chaos. They send 1 inquisitor, 1 interrogator and 10 tactical marines to cover the entire of the inside of mount Everest plus the giant tower built on it. Don’t worry it only takes them a couple of hours to clear it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What weapons proved effective in the war in Ukraine?
Answer: The most underestimated weapon before the war, was the humble FPV drone. This was considered to be an insurgent and improvised weapon, mostly famous for it’s use by islamist fundamentalists in Syria such as ISIS. The AFU had put their money into TB-2 Bayraktar drones after their success against Armenia. However, the TB-2 is largely a failure in the conflict. While much successful footage came out initially, the reality is that practically 100% of TB-2s were destroyed, and quite early as well. On the contrary, the cheap FPV drones which became popularized by Chechen veterans from Syria, quickly evolved from dropping small grenades, to carrying full size RPG warheads and being supplied at an industrial level. Already in December 2022, western analysts were raising alarm over the success of these inexpensive weapons. The most successful one is the more expensive Lancet type drone which is in fact a purpose build military kamikaze drone. Unlike the FPV drone it has a serious and multipurpose warhead, and the newer versions have AI assistance and a range of over 45km. So far, there has been 1,195 Lancet hits confirmed through video evidence as counted by lostarmour, including 262 tank hits. 114 confirmed hits from the helicopter launched LMUR. 28 confirmed hits from KUB-BLA. But this pales in comparison to the fact, that the Russian forces have also conducted at least 3,945 hits with smaller FPV drones of which there is video evidence, about half of these are on vehicles crews leaving their disabled tanks, infantry or defensive positions. These hit counts do not include grenades dropped from drones. It should also be noted that the AFU use FPV drones, but I was unable to find a comprehensive list of hits and video evidence from them. Also famously they use naval kamikaze drones to strike Russian ships and shore targets. I think this venue of weaponry is the one that has been proved to work the most in practice during this conflict. Though we will likely see an electronic counter to them, something which is already emerging.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: The Americans usually called in artillery strikes. How did the Soviets and the British typically overcome German machine gun nests with overlapping fields of fire?
Answer: If by Americans using artillery you mean heavy howitzer fire, this is likely not the case. The Americans might have called in mortars, and their widespread us of portable radios made on-call artillery at all levels a possibility. As for the Soviets, they did not have the widespread use of radios, so using artillery on surprise machine guns they encountered would not have been a viable option for everyone. Instead the Soviets made excellent use of combined arms tactics, particularly in the late war. The Su-76 for example was a self propelled gun that was designed to provide support to infantry formations. During an assault the assaulting infantry were basically always reinforced with support equipment, at least since Stalingrad. The support equipment usually included a tank, or something like an Su-76, but in some cases like assaults against heavily fortified positions, could also go all the way up to the heavy 152mm SPG ISU-152. The Soviets favored direct fire, because it enabled the gunners to correct their own shots, though it was riskier than indirect fire, the vehicles like ISU-152 and Su-76 were armored against what they were expected to face. The British like the Americans likely relied on mortars and had them on call, and in some cases might have had 25 pounder guns, which are roughly equivalent in firepower to the Su-76 or ZiS-3 towed cannon. It should also be noted that infantry tactics in all the armies did not require heavy support elements. Infantry at the squad level were tried to fight machine gun positions through basic fire and maneuver infantry tactics, in which one element distracts the machine gun with suppressive fire while the other move into a position in which they could use grenade to destroy it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are war games a good way to prepare for an actual war?
Answer: Yes, war games are an excellent tool for training for war. War games when done right, are able to simulate very accurately many decisions made by officers at all kinds of level. They can simulate technology, economy, intelligence, imperfect orders, delay, command structures, political objectives and team work between officers. And this is probably exactly why war games are played by military officers. I wrote a PhD proposal to introduce war games as a form of teaching and studying international relations to students at universities in Denmark, unfortunately no one was interested in this. But I would maintain it remains a great combination of game theory and simulation with human elements. We know from WW2, that wargamers could in real time simulate combat scenarios like those faced by British convoys, and anticipate the moves of German submarines and then radio back solutions to British destroyers. Do not underestimate the power of simulating scenarios before trying them in real life.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How did the Poles treated Germans and Russians in their territories acquired as a result of ww1? There are some claims that the actions led to Nazi-Soviet pack to invade and divide Poland and the Katyn massacre.
Answer: According to realist international relations theory, the treatment of Germans or Russians would not greatly affect the decision to invade a country. Indeed I would say this is also the case here. Poland also did not acquire the territory due to World War 1, but due to the Polish intervention in the Russian-civil war, as the Polish attacked the Red Army, after it took control of Vilnius following the withdrawal of German forces from the area. Poland fared surprisingly well in the Soviet-Polish war and ended up with a considerable part of Belarus under occupation as well as parts of Ukraine. Due to the ongoing Russian civil war, the Soviets were essentially forced to sign a peace treaty on these unfavorable terms, which satisfied no one really, as the Polish had hoped for a great realm connected to both the Baltic and black sea, while the Soviets had hoped for total control of the former Russian Empire. At this point a future conflict was guaranteed. In 1939 the Soviets recaptured the territory of Belarus and Ukraine from Poland as well as some minor additions. The reason for this was not due to how people were treated in these areas, but because the Soviets did not want part of Ukraine or Belarus in foreign hands. Likewise, the treatment of Germans in Poland was completely irrelevant to the Germans. After WW1 some territories of historical Germany was given to Poland and Germany wanted these territories back, additionally as part of the Nazi ideology the Poles were considered sub-human and ideal slave labor, as such the plan was to also exploit the remaining part of Poland for the benefit of Germans until they no longer needed them at which point the plan was to exterminate the remaining Poles to allow for a great German Empire, which of course also included much of the USSR. The Katyn massacre and other acts of repression from the Soviets were not carried out as a form of revenge either. This was due to the Soviets wanting to attain control over the areas quickly, and this was done through repressing those who were class enemies in the Soviet view, as well as eliminating those which the Soviets considered could form the cadre of a Polish resistance or alternative government. As such, officers, government officials and civil servants were cynically targeted to prevent such a revolutionary core from forming. It had very little to do with ethnicity, and quite a lot to do with expediency of establishing the Soviet control. Not that the Polish government was as popular in Belarus as modern Polish historians try to revise history to show, George Sanford(2005) in his book Katyn and the Soviet Massacre of 1940, notes that following the German invasion local militias in western Belarus spontaneously started fighting with the Polish army, killing as many as 2,500 Polish soldiers and border guards. On the contrary no spontaneous militias were formed to fight the Soviets. Though all of this Pales in the comparison of the brutality that the Germans showed in their advance, killing at least 6,000 civilians in the bombing of Warsaw the following assault on Warsaw killed an additional 18,000 civilians, due to casual brutality of the Nazis around 200,000 civilians were killed by the Germans in the invasion roughly 5,700 per day.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: The US got a T-90A that Ukraine captured. What do they hope to learn from it? Its only the T-90A from the 90s with some improved thermals. The T-90MS is the one they would get Intel from not a T-90A.
Answer: The US did indeed receive a T-90A which was captured in Ukraine, what they can learn from it? Well if nothing else they can cut the armour apart and see what the state of Russian armor development was when the T-90A was made, if it has any surprises and such. But that probably is not as interesting as the fact that a T-90M was already captured last year including all the newest Russian electronics, loading systems, ammunition, gun barrel technology etc. It is very likely that America possess near perfect knowledge of the Russian state of armor development of the second newest generation, the newest being the T-14 which is yet to see combat. So for all intends and purposes Russian armor which is currently operating holds no secrets. The T-90MS is less sophisticated than the T-90M by the way. That’s just how it is.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: With the recent conflicts in Europe and the Middle East (in the early 2020s), is there a trend, a necessity to whitewash the crimes of the Nazis during WWII?
Answer: There is, as we say in history, a battle for the memory of WW2 and Nazis. This battle did not begin recently, it has been ongoing ever since WW2 ended. This is true both in Europe and the Middle East. The tendency to whitewash or the tendency to expose has gone up and down in Europe, while in the Middle East it has remained fairly steady. When you say “European conflicts” I am guessing you mean Ukraine. Ukraine has indeed had a tendency to whitewash the OUN in particular, the Ukrainian Nazi auxiliaries from WW2. However, this is not due to a recent conflict. In fact this tendency is strong associated with nationalism in general, and began practically on the day the USSR fell apart. OUN leader, Stepan Bandera, was indeed made into a national hero in Ukraine, where he was officially awarded the title post-humously. However, this happened in 2010 and the decision was Viktor Yushchenko’s, not Zelensky’s. Additionally, it would be unfair to not point out that such whitewashing has happened many other places in Europe too. I personally witnessed people quite happily celebrating the Arrow Cross organization in Budapest last time i visited, on the middle of the main stream leading to the parliament, with no one batting an eye. Likewise in my own country, the complicity of Danes in Nazi atrocities is generally not acknowledged at all, vile SS Nazi and known murderer Søren Kam, escaped Justice his entire life, with no serious efforts even made to have him prosecuted until 2006, despite his identity and crimes being known since the 1970s. As for the middle east, anti-semitism has been omnipresent for quite a long time, much longer than the current conflict. The white washing of Nazis was essential for many middle eastern countries for various reasons. First of all, the fact that millions of innocent Jews were murdered for their ethnicity, is not able to coincide with the idea that Jews are colonizers and collectively responsible for many problems all over the middle east, as as been the narrative promoted by many of the dictatorships that until recently ruled much of the Arab speaking world. For example, al-Liwaa al-Islami, the ruling party of Egypt’s official newspaper, published in 2004 an article called "The Lie About the Burning of the jews" by Dr. Rif'at Sayyed Ahmad. In 2006, Lebanese New TV employed this strategy. The channel broadcast a show where it was stated that Holocaust scholar Raul Hilberg had said only 50,000 jews had died in WW2, which of course Raul Hilberg never said. The holocaust has also been outright denied by the official Syrian government news paper, Syria Times, in 2000, and by al-Manar in 1999. Which I believe is owned by Hezbollah operating out of Lebanon. Hamas on the other hand, has the official view, that the holocaust was organized by the Jews themselves in order to make Jews move to Palestine, this was stated in al-Risala in 2003. Now that isn’t to say that everyone in the middle east have been trying to whitewash Nazis or deny holocaust, in 2006 the recent comments and groups attempting to do just this, outraged Kuwaiti Journalist Khaled al-Janfawi who said: Holding a conference devoted to Holocaust denial reflects a lack of cultural and human sensitivity which may exacerbate hatred among human beings. [...] We Muslims need to display human, cultural, and moral sensitivity in order to be a positive force in a humane world that no longer tolerates ethnic and religious conflict. We must stay away from anything that generates conflict among human beings. [...] Holding a Holocaust [denial] conference in Iran is adding fuel to the fire. [...] Some of the participants were agitators, and [others] were [individuals] involved in racist discrimination against [minorities] other than the Jews, such as the African -Americans in the U.S Likewise, intellectuals in Tunesia, Morroco and Algeria expressed similar views and disgust at the historical revisionism. The most outrageous examples apart from Iran, are those countries who had previously fought with Israel militarily. Which is not really surprising. Much of the whitewashing of Nazis are left overs of the Arab-Israeli wars. And while it is flaring up now, it is not because of a recent tendency to do this, but because of the long standing political context in the middle east, of viewing everything related to Jews to being about Israel in actuality. The tendencies to promote or fight whitewashing is a rather fluid thing, shaped by governments, media and historians, and not something the average person can really be blamed for. For this post I consulted the papers: Mikael Tossavainen, 2008, The Holocaust In Arab Public Discourse: Historicized Politics And Politicized History, JSTOR Gilbert Achcar, 2020, Holocaust Denial in Western and Arab Contexts, Journal of Palestine Studies

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: In your opinion, do you think the axis powers were taken back by the belligerent response of the allies since their actions (genocide, resource exploitation, etc) basically mirrored what the allies were doing or had done a few decades ago?
Answer: The Axis powers were fully aware of their actions being vile, disgusting and inhumane. During the Wannsee Conference, when the final solution (holocaust) was quite literally planned and agreed on by high ranking Nazi leaders, the stenographer was ordered to stop writing the minutes of the meeting, if anyone started being clear about murdering Jews. They did this because they knew it was criminal and evil, and did not want there to be evidence of what they were planning on doing. Even the sanitized minutes of the meeting were supposed to be destroyed, but one copy survived due to someone keeping it against the rules. Eichman’s List of Jews still to be eliminated I reject the notion that the allies had done similar things prior to WW2. I am quite famously critical of imperialism and colonialism, and there are genocides and other atrocities to talk about. Most of which were carried out in gross negligence or casual cruelty in general. However, this kinda of industrial murder was a unheard of, and we should not forget that Jews were not the only victims of the Nazis. The Nazis might have taken inspiration, from US race laws for example, but what they did was incomparable in terms of atrocities. That isn’t to say I think that the any of the countries which fought against Germany and Japan were innocent by a long shot, but they were nothing relative to what Germany and Japan brought upon the world in just 6 years.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Because the Soviet Union was resource independent, would it ever make sense for Stalin to attack Hitler first? (assuming Germany doesn't attack.) The risk vs reward is so much lower for Soviet's to attack first.
Answer: The Soviet Union was not resource independent, though they wanted to be and worked towards it. Never the less, the Soviets wanted to attack Nazi Germany. From 1934 to 1939 the Soviets tried to establish a way to destroy Nazi Germany before they were fully armed, having understood Hitler’s ultimate intentions quite well. Litvinov pursued a collective anti-Nazi alliance for 5 years before WW2. Additionally, and quite contrary to popular belief, the Soviet Union had appointed Maxim Litvinov, as the foreign secretary, a firm and true believer in collective security, and even disarmament. Litvinov improved the standing of the USSR considerably and tried very hard to build alliances with very hostile countries like the USA, UK and France. The USA not even having recognized the USSR as a legitimate state until 1933, when Litvinov convinced them otherwise. I am mentioning all this, because Litvinov was no figurehead, but a true driver of Soviet foreign policy, and in 1935 he accomplished a security agreement with France and Czechoslovakia. This was clearly aimed at Germany, but there were two big problems. Firstly France never fully committed to it, secondly Soviet troops could not easily arrive in France nor Czechoslovakia in case Germany attacked, neither could they directly engage the Nazis as they did not border them. This meant that the USSR needed a military access assurance from either Poland or Romania which did not arrive in 1935, and further didn’t arrive in any subsequent discussion of European collective security. It should be noted that until 1939 Poland was quite close to Nazi Germany, having immediately signed a non-aggression pact in 1934, and as late as 31st of October 1938 the Polish Ambassador in Berlin was discussing with Von Ribbentrop interesting things like breaking up the remaining Czechoslovakia and emigration of Jews. Indeed Polish leadership had envisioned Poland as a rising power of central Europe, but had lost out on the ability to influence Hungary, Slovakia and Romania. Rather than seeing the writing on the wall however, Poland decided to rely entirely on France and Britain for security, and continued to refuse Soviet aid in the case of war, unable to settle it’s differences. After 5 years of rejections to form the coalition against Nazism, the Soviets perceived the intentions of the western countries + Poland, as being overtly anti-Soviet, suspecting (quite rightly for the most part) that the western countries were hoping that a German-Soviet war would be the outcome, and would allow them to sit back and watch their European rivals destroy each other. Famously the caused the Soviets to sign a fateful treaty with Germany instead. It would have made perfect sense to attack Hitler first, but geographically the Soviets were never able to do that until after the Germans had taken Poland anyway. The Soviets did not wish to fight Germany alone, and was unable to secure any collective security treaties from the western powers. As such it never happened, though they very much wanted to.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What current trends in media (film, TV, music, video games, publishing and social media) in North and Eastern Europe have not yet emerged in Western Europe and North America?
Answer: Yes there is, that trend is technical realism. I can’t speak for everything, but from what I have seen, something which is clearly a high priority in many media products including games and movies in eastern Europe is technical realism. By that I mean that the physics and the mechanics of the products made are clearly quite well thought out. Probably the game i spend the most time in, is War Thunder, and the reason for that is because I enjoy the vehicles. Does the game actually make sense? No not really, it’s just a big bad of vehicles senselessly fighting each other. However, there is essentially no western competitor who could even dream of making a game like it. If we look at other video games like DCS World, Men of War, Gates of Hell or the upcoming Broken Arrow, these are similarly east European games with a high level of technical realism. Most of them unrivaled in their field. There are many examples of movies made in eastern Europe, Russia in particular, which have a high technical realism, such as Paniflov’s 28, T-34 and even older movies like Waterloo from 1970 which had fantastic detail in the technical aspects. In my opinion it appears quite obvious, that technical realism is really not a high priority in NA and EU in terms of entertainment, I enjoy these aspects, but many games are very cartoonish, and the pseudo-realism of Call of Duty is kind of nauseating. Likewise even tacticool movies like John Wick, still has not realized basic concept of how suppressors work, and while there are many cool aspects in the movies, there are many technically very silly ones too despite this actually being the main allure of the franchise. I always felt that there was a certain assumption that the viewer in modern western products is more ignorant than they really are, so they wouldn’t appreciate realism in details, which is sad, because this was once a high consideration before we even had CGI.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What would the effect be on Russia's military capability if they continue to lose tanks at the current rate?
Answer: The Oryx claim of Russian losses currently stands at 2.577 tanks over a span of 2 years. That would be 1289 tanks per year. The current Russian production is estimated at 800 refurbishments and 300 new production models per year which is probably exclusively T-90M. This means that the Russian production essentially covers the losses pretty well. Some tanks have been brought out of storage as is to cover the gaps, such as T-62M and T-80U tanks. Of course the actual loss rate is probably not what Oryx claims, as Oryx assigns every unverifiable tank as a Russian loss, including T-72M and T-64 models, which are likely Ukrainian losses not Russian. A good example is the above picture, which is counted as a Russian tank loss. That certainly is not clear from the picture to me. It is impossible to accurate identify this tank at all based on this picture. Either way, Russian tank losses has slowed down while the production has gone up, and they still have plenty of tanks in storage. So likely a loss rate at current rates, would not be an issue for the Russian Army.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why did Revolutions like those in France, Russia, Cuba, Iran, etc. come under attack from the 'Western powers/powers that be' when they occur?
Answer: There are two principle reasons why revolutions come under attack, and while in more modern scenarios people will often find complicated reasons to justify the same reactions, I find it merely a cover. To arrive at the essence of why, we can look at the French revolution for a more honest take that was not quite as covered in modern propaganda as political justifications are now. In 1791 almost immediately after the French revolution, the Declaration of Pillnitz, was issued by Leopold II of Austria and Holy Roman Emperor, as well as Frederick William II of Prussia. The statement read as follows: His Majesty the Emperor and His Majesty the King of Prussia (…) declare together that they regard the actual situation of His Majesty the King of France as a matter of communal interest for all sovereigns of Europe. They hope that that interest will be recognized by the powers whose assistance is called in, and that they won't refuse, together with aforementioned Majesties, the most efficacious means for enabling the French king to strengthen, in utmost liberty, the foundations of a monarchical government suiting to the rights of the sovereigns and favourable to the well-being of the French. In that case, aforementioned Majesties are determined to act promptly and unanimously, with the forces necessary for realizing the proposed and communal goal. In expectation, they will give the suitable orders to their troops so that they will be ready to commence activity. That is the entire reason for the beginning of what would become the Napoleonic wars. It’s quite simple. The Kings of Europe, particularly Austria and Prussia, did not like the idea of ordinary people deposing a king, no matter how bad he was. As such it was a matter of communal interest for all the “sovereigns of Europe”, as in the rulers. Simply put, the privileged ruling class never likes the idea of a revolution and want every one of them to fail. This is the domestic policy reason. The second simple reason, is the foreign policy one. If a revolution happens, likely the alliances of that country will be broken, trade deal nullified and everything up for re-consideration. If you are a foreign power gaining something from your relationship with that country, you are against that revolution, if you are a foreign power and an enemy or rival of that country you are for it. For example, if France had a revolution now, made by extreme right wing people trying to create the France proper by kicking out the “non French”, it would simply not be allowed by NATO, it would be considered undemocratic fascist junta and it would be destroyed by military force if necessary. Without a doubt. However, if Russia had a revolution, made by extreme right wing people trying to create Russia proper by removing the minority republics from Russia, it would be entirely different matter for NATO, it would be the collective will of the people, and Russia as a multi cultural empire was due to fracture into ethnic states, such a thing could be supported entirely naturally, for the sake of democracy. And that is essentially the two reasons for every support or opposition to any revolution in history.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are tank guns as good as a 155mm howitzer?
Answer: Tank guns like the 125mm and 120mm standard smoothbore tank guns of the east and west, generate way more chamber pressure than most howitzer guns do which fire their shells at slower speeds generally speaking. For example the 155mm M777 howitzer fires shells at 827 m/s muzzle velocity. In comparison the 125mm tank guns, can fire APFSDS ammunition at up to 1,800 m/s. This means that tank barrels have to be able to withstand quite a lot of pressure. As such guns like the 125mm 2A46M has a service life of about 450 shots with APFSDS, up to 1,200 shots with full caliber ammunition, compare this with the 1,500–2,500 shots with the M777 howitzer before a barrel change is needed. In that sense howitzers are able to fire more rounds of a higher power. If you are asking if a 155mm howitzer is more powerful than a 120–125mm tank gun in terms of explosive power, the answer is yes they are.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: The T-64, T-72, T-80 and T-90 all have 125mm main guns, but are they basically the same and use the same ammo?
Answer: The 125mm series of guns installed on these tanks are similar, but they are not the same and do not perform the same. There are many minor improvements to the gun over it’s life, but we can talk about the two main variants. The 2A46 and the 2A46M. The 2A46 suffered from accuracy issues, which were largely addressed with the 2A46M. Firstly as seen from above, the barrel became seated on the thermal sleve with more points of contact, which reduced inconsistent performance when the barrel heated up. The 2A46 featured a recoil buffer on the lower right of the gun breach, which swayed the gun slightly during firing. This meant that the 2A46 had a tendency to fire slightly to the side of the aim point. Not a terrible amount at normal ranges, but enough to affect accuracy at long range. However, this was fixed on the 2A46M by making two recoil buffers spreading the recoil between and upper right and lower left recoil buffer. Additionally the 2A46M featured a new breech block, gun cradle, and a new barrel with an interrupted screw which permitted quick swapping the barrel out the front of the tank in field conditions, with 2 hours without the need for removing the turret or advanced machines. Essentially almost every part of the gun was in fact changed, and resulted in drastically higher accuracy, life span, and ease of maintenance. The actual improvements of the 2A46M-5 which is what is currently used on the T-72B3, T-80BVM and T-90 tanks, are not entirely known. Likely they are aimed at improving service life, but other features might be present. All 125mm guns are backwards compatible, but older guns might not be able to shoot the newest ammunition, but it wouldn’t matter much anyway, as the newest ammunition requires a newer auto loader anyway.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How would the original M1 Abrams fair in combat vs. its Soviet Russian contemporaries?
Answer: The original M1 Abrams is not the version which exists in the minds of most when they talk about this famous vehicle. The one most people are familiar with is the M1A1 or M1A2 which are not the original versions of the tank. The M1 differed from later versions quite significantly due to its lack of a 120mm gun and thinner armor that also lacked no depleted uranium. In terms of armor the original M1 Abrams had roughly a 350mm RHAe frontal arc protection, as opposed to the M1A1 with a 400mm and the M1A2 with a 600mm RHAe vs kinetic penetrators. Substantially more against HEAT. The Soviet contemporary would be the T-80B. The T-80B had a frontal arc protection of 500 RHAe, significantly better than the original M1. In terms of weaponry, the M1 had the L7 105mm rifled cannon, which was obsolete by the 1980s, which was entirely acknowledged by the USA who were trying to procure 120mm guns for the M1 but they were not ready when the M1 was, so the first 120mm gun armed Abrams were not fielded until 1985. The T-80B had a 125mm gun, with significantly more power than 105mm gun. The M735 was the standard APFSDS round for the US 105mm gun armed tanks in the 1980s, it began production in 1978 a year before the M1 and was designed for the M1 and M60A3 tanks to increase their effectiveness. According to US tests the M735 which was the standard, was completely inadequate for penetrating the T-80B, even the newer M833 which was not available to the M1 initially was inadequate. While the Soviet 125mm gun with the ammunition the American were aware of, was deemed able to destroy the M1 and even M1A1 from the front. Hence why later M1s were given DU armor. You can observe the chart below. In terms of mobility the T-80B and the M1 Abrams were both excellent. In terms of day time optics both had very good magnification. In terms of night time optics the M1 had a significantly better suite, with it’s thermal optics, though it’s nothing like what you see today. The T-80 also had one extra trick up it’s sleeve, the ability to fire Kobra ATGMs allowing it to engage like an anti tank guided missile launcher, at a range of at least 4km, twice what is considered the effective kinetic engagement range at the time which is 2km. In short: the Soviet contemporary had significant armor and firepower advantages over the initial M1 Abrams. Of course either tank could destroy each other under the right circumstances, but the M1 would have essentially no real protection from the front, which is a massive disadvantage.

Question: Does Russia use T-54/55 tanks instead of newer models like the T-72 and T-90? If so, why?
Answer: Russia does not use the T-54 or T-55 tanks instead of any other tank neither the T-72 nor the T-90. These tanks are used in the traditional tank role, and Russia has a large storage of T-72s even now. However, Russia is confirmed to use the T-55 tanks in a different role, namely that of remote controlled bomb. Since a tank even if it is an old one is difficult to destroy without anti tank weapons, they make dangerous VBIEDs. The T-55 is filled with explosives then rolled across fields towards Ukrainian positions. So far it appears that this has not been particularly successful however, the fields are still littered with anti tank mines, and often the VBIED T-55 gets stuck on these, and then destroyed with RPGs or other weapons before reaching the AFU trench line. Question: North Korea has for many decades been producing tank and artillery shells identical in caliber to those used by the Russian army. Question: How many shells have been produced in North Korea?
Answer: There is absolutely no way to tell this for certain, we don’t even know how many artillery guns and other weapons North Korea really have. However, the North Korean doctrine was to win a conventional war using overwhelming artillery fire power, and prolonged determination. While North Korea has likely built these for a long time, and potentially continuously, North Korea also has a limited industry. That being said, North Korea likely has stockpiles in the millions of shells, potentially double digit millions of shells. Not all of them are in calibers commonly used by Russia though, for example the Koksan shown above, uses a 170mm shell, while the similar Russian 2S7M Malka uses 203mm shells. So while they appear very similar, they would not be able to exchange shells. 152mm and 122mm shells as well as 122mm Grad rockets are likely to be the kind of products that most readily can be used by Russia. Another caveat is that North Korean ammunition likely uses TNT rather an A-IX-2 explosive filler, meaning that they will not have quite the same firepower as modern shells.

Question: How significant is the reported advance of the Freedom of Russia Legion, the Russian Volunteer Corps, and the Sibir Battalion into Kursk and Belgorod Oblasts?
Answer: This advance is a PR stunt and not really an advance at all. Essentially it consists of a skirmish that didn’t go so well for the AFU at the border checkpoint, it is also not the first fight there. It was followed by a fake claim that AFU troops were deep inside Russian territory, supported by a video of a couple of soldiers on an empty street. Unfortunately for this footage is from the Ukrainian village of Ryzhevka, in the Sumy region, which itself was occupied by the Russians in 2022 and similarly used for propaganda purposes. In the border crossing attempt, which was filmed almost in its entirety, two Ukrainian T-64BV tanks fired at an empty building and two random objects, before being disabled by a mine and later destroyed by Chechen national guard unit with a grenade from a drone. By my estimation this T-64BV managed to cross about 50m over the check point, the crew can be seen running back across the border after it was tracked. The second tank did not cross the border, but instead retreated upon seeing the first tank on fire. There were no Russian troops present at the border check point, instead the border troops being Chechen, watched the whole thing from the air and naturally put it on tiktok immediately. This advance was a small scale attempt to generate support for the Ukrainian course, and maybe also put some pressure on the Russian public during their election time. But being caught faking the location is a PR nightmare, though many will simply deny it, one can just look at google earth images from the location I mentioned it see for themselves. It is important for Ukraine to generate some victories in order to persuade western backers who are not delivering the promised aid, but I think this was a very silly way of going about it, and probably will adversely affect the course more than anything else.

Question: During WWII, if Germans had attacked the Kursk salient in May 1943 before the Soviets had fortified the area, would it have been successful?
Answer: If the Germans had attacked earlier there would have been fewer Soviet fortifications. There would also have been fewer Germans. There would have been far fewer German tanks, and practically no Panthers. The terrain would still have been muddy, and it’s not like the Soviets didn’t have any fortifications at all. The Germans would still have been hit by a massive counter attack, and unlike in the real scenario, they would also have been fighting against the mud season of the area getting stuck horribly. Attacking sooner would not really have yielded many advantages to the Germans, which is why they didn’t. Despite all the memes about Hitler making every decision, the German military was aware that such an offensive would likely have failed.

Question: If a grey knight shows up on a world in Warhammer 40k, how screwed are you?
Answer: Not as fucked as you might think. One of the things I do like about warhammer is that it has quite a lot of room for sensible use of force. Essentially in warhammer, imperial organizations tend to respond to threats as they can, for example in Eisenhorn the Ordo Xenos fights chaos because they are the ones who are around, and in Gate of Bones, Custodes arrive on a planet to fight a fairly small number of chaos forces which were battles a single guards regiment, they arrive supported by 3 entire battle-fleets, which is quite the overkill, but they are the ones who are they so that’s what you get. This is actually very reasonable, the Grey Knights wouldn’t stop themselves from fighting a foe of the empire, simply because it wasn’t a great enough demon. Though on the other hand they might kill you afterwards simply for knowing they exist.

Question: During the Cold War, just like how people in the Eastern Bloc emigrated to the Western Bloc to escape communism, were there also some people who emigrated from the Western Bloc to the Eastern Bloc to escape capitalism?
Answer: It is information which is quite difficult to search for, but it did indeed happen. From Denmark, Martin Andersen Nexø decided to move to East Germany in 1951, where he lived in Dresden until he died in 1954 (Age 84). He is probably the second most famous Danish author after H.C. Anderson, and his book Pelle Eroberen, is the most translated Danish work after Anderson as well, it is also a great book in my opinion by the way. It was made into a movie as well where no other than Max von Sydow plays one of the title roles (The priest from the exorcist, Blofeld from James Bond) Ollie Harrington, a famous American cartoonist and civil rights activist moved to East Germany in 1961 after his friend Richard Wright died. Harrington suspected that the US government were targeting black US civil rights advocates for assassination, he lived in East Germany until his death in 1995. Wolfgang Gans zu Putlitz an active anti-nazi resistance member before WW2, and British spy, and witness at the Nuremberg trials, defected to East Germany in 1954 out of disgust for the West German establishment and their rehabilitation of Nazi warcriminals. Perhaps one of the most famous cases is Ursel Lorenzen, a secretary at the NATO HQ from 1966 to 1979 passed essentially all NATO battle plans to the Soviet Union and defected to East Germany in 1979. Her whereabouts to this date is unknown. These are just some examples, generally speaking the USSR did not encourage obvious defection in the same way the west did. The west literally paid people to leave the Eastern Bloc countries and would take just about anyone for the propaganda victory. The Soviet approach was vastly different, they preferred their agents to stay inside western countries and collect data. The people defecting to the USSR tended to stay put, and work for the ideological course undercover. The Soviet spy network was well known to be vast, it included the Cambridge five, which were a British spy ring that were top placed in Mi5, and other very embarrassing positions. Those cultured enough have seen “Yes Minister” will remember Bernard saying: Well if I know it, I am sure the Russians know it. The Kremlin usually gets NATO defense information before it filters to us at Number 10 (British Prime Minister residence)
